tldr: A proposal for GraphOp-WM, a graph-structured world model capable of zero-shot prediction and control even when physical robot parameters like link lengths and masses change. By explicitly factorizing motion dynamics into a morphology-independent local dynamics basis and a morphology-conditioned structured operator, it achieves strong generalization to unseen parameters.
overview:
In deep reinforcement learning, world models that simulate environment behavior are powerful tools. However, existing world models suffer from a major weakness: their predictive accuracy degrades sharply when morphology parameters, such as robot mass, link lengths, or joint damping, change. Standard morphology-conditioning methods typically feed these parameters into the network as a single context vector. This leaves the physical division of labor ambiguous within the learned model—it is unclear which part of the motion is morphology-independent and reusable, and which part should adapt to parameter shifts.

To address this, the authors focus on a graph structure where robot links (rigid bodies) serve as nodes and joints or actuators serve as edges. They propose GraphOp-WM, which explicitly factorizes a single-step transition into the product of a morphology-independent local dynamics basis and a morphology-conditioned structured operator that describes motion propagation based on static morphology parameters.

Furthermore, the authors introduce a controlled MuJoCo benchmark across Hopper, Walker2d, and HalfCheetah with systematically scaled geometry, mass, damping, and gear ratios. They evaluate generalization across interpolation, out-of-distribution extrapolation, and held-out parameter compositions. The results show that decoupling physical coupling structures into operators enables robust generalization in both prediction and model predictive control (MPC) for unseen robot morphologies.
contributions: Formulated the problem setting and challenges of generalizing dynamics prediction and planning across morphology-parameter variations within robot families.
Proposed a factorized architecture that separates transitions into a morphology-independent local dynamics basis and a structured operator based on kinematic trees.
Established a training mechanism using architectural information separation, basis normalization, and paired-morphology supervision to firmly route morphology dependence into the operator pathway.
Defined a systematic evaluation benchmark covering parameter interpolation, extrapolation, and held-out compositions in Hopper, Walker2d, and HalfCheetah.

sections.heading: Why Do Existing World Models Struggle with Physical Body Changes?
sections.summary: While world models achieve strong control performance on fixed robots, they are vulnerable to parameter shifts like link lengths and masses. This section points out the limitations of feeding morphology information as a mere input vector and presents a new design philosophy that explicitly separates reusable local motions from morphology-driven coupling changes.
sections.details:
Recent world models like DreamerV3 and TD-MPC2 have enabled sample-efficient continuous control by learning latent transitions of the environment. However, most assume a single fixed robot model. When robot link lengths, link masses, joint damping, or actuator gear ratios change, the model's predictive accuracy degrades sharply.

Existing multi-robot research has explored passing robot specifications or embeddings to models as input conditions. However, simply concatenating a context vector fails to clarify which parts of the transition remain invariant across morphologies and which parts should alter coupling based on physical parameters.

Articulated robots possess clear physical structures. Even if limbs are made slightly longer or heavier, the fundamental local dynamical response rules experienced by each rigid body remain the same. What actually changes is how motion propagates from one body to another across joints—the strength and pattern of coupling.

Therefore, this paper proposes GraphOp-WM, a graph-structured world model that explicitly separates reusable local dynamics from structured coupling operators governed by morphology parameters. By treating rigid bodies as nodes and joints as edges, the model multiplies a base increment predicted by a local kernel with a structured operator generated from static morphology parameters, aiming for resilient generalization across unseen parameters.

sections.heading: Mapping Prior Research and Positioning GraphOp-WM
sections.summary: This section organizes related work across four domains: world models, morphology-conditioned models, modular policies, and graph physics simulators. GraphOp-WM stands out by modeling morphology parameters not as black-box features, but as physical operators responsible for motion propagation.
sections.details:
To clarify where this work stands, related literature can be grouped into four categories:

- World models for continuous control:
Evolving from early works like PETS and MBPO to DreamerV3 for long-horizon latent rollouts, and TD-MPC or TD-MPC2 combining short-horizon planning with terminal value estimation. GraphOp-WM adopts TD-MPC's planning and control interface while factorizing the internal transition function to reflect physical structures.

- Morphology-conditioned world models:
While methods like CaDM and MAMBA infer latent context from interaction histories, robot geometry and mass are usually known beforehand via design files such as MJCF or URDF. Approaches like QWM and WestWorld encode known robot specifications, but mostly rely on a single pooled vector or Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) routing signals. GraphOp-WM fundamentally differs by treating parameters as coupling matrices that act on local responses.

- Morphology-adaptive control policies:
Methods such as NerveNet, Shared Modular Policies (SMP), MetaMorph, and Body Transformer treat body structures as graphs and share policy network weights. These primarily aim at policy transfer, whereas GraphOp-WM targets the transfer of the environment dynamics prediction model.

- Graph dynamics and operator learning:
Works like Interaction Networks and GNS use Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) for physics modeling, and some combine them with Koopman operators. GraphOp-WM adopts an operator formulation explicitly incorporating kinematic tree incidence matrices, balancing physical interpretability with extrapolation capability.

sections.heading: The Goal: Zero-Shot Adaptation Within the Same Robot Family
sections.summary: The control problem, where state and action dimensions can vary across morphologies, is formulated using graph representations. The paper focuses on zero-shot prediction and planning for unseen physical parameter variants within articulated robot families sharing a common topology.
sections.details:
This study considers a family of continuous control problems characterized by a morphology index $m$. Each morphology $m$ is represented as an attributed graph $\mathcal{G}_m = (\mathcal{V}_m, \mathcal{E}_m^{\mathrm{joint}}, \mathcal{E}_m^{\mathrm{act}})$. Here, nodes $i \in \mathcal{V}_m$ denote rigid links carrying geometric and inertial metadata. Edges represent joints and actuators, encoding kinematic connectivity and action mappings.

During training, trajectory data collected from a set of training morphologies $\mathcal{M}_{\mathrm{train}}$ is utilized. At evaluation time, zero-shot state transition prediction and MPC planning performance are evaluated on unseen test morphologies $\mathcal{M}_{\mathrm{test}}$.

Crucially, evaluation is carefully categorized into parameter interpolation, out-of-distribution extrapolation, and compositional held-out splits where multiple parameter changes occur simultaneously. Universal transfer across entirely different topologies—such as from a quadruped to a snake robot—is outside the scope of this work; the focus is strictly on parameter generalization within families sharing link connectivity.

sections.heading: An Architecture Decoupling Local Bases from Structured Operators
sections.summary: This section explains the core method of GraphOp-WM. Transitions are factorized into a static-attribute-blind local basis and a structured operator generated from static attributes. Paired-morphology supervision ensures morphology influences are properly isolated into the operator.
sections.details:
The GraphOp-WM pipeline is built upon the following fine-grained physical inductive biases:

4.1 Morphology Graph Construction:
Attributes for rigid body nodes and joint edges are extracted from MuJoCo XML definitions. Nodes receive static attributes like geom types, sizes, masses, and principal moments of inertia. Edges hold joint types, rotation axes, position offsets, damping coefficients, and gear ratios. Dynamic states (local positions, orientations, velocities, contact flags) are also assigned to corresponding nodes and edges.

4.2 State Tokens and Information Separation:
The dynamic state of each rigid body is mapped to a token $z_{t,i}$ via a shared encoder. In a crucial design choice, static morphology parameters like masses and link lengths are withheld from this encoder. This physically prevents static individual differences from leaking into the dynamic state representation. Global readouts combine an attention mechanism with learnable queries and the root link token.

4.3 Morphology-Independent Local Dynamics Basis:
A local kernel predicts base motion increments for each link. This kernel inspects only its own dynamic state, connected joint dynamic features, and actuator inputs, remaining blind to static morphology parameters. Candidate increments are root-mean-square (RMS) normalized to remove scale ambiguity, yielding a shared basis $\bar{B}_t$.

4.4 Structured Morphology Operator:
A morphology encoder processing only static graph attributes produces node scaling factors $d_m$, edge couplings $w_m$, and low-rank global modes $\tilde{U}_m, s_m$. These are gated by current posture and contact states to assemble the operator $\mathcal{A}_{m,t}$, consisting of three components:
1. A diagonal term (local response of the rigid body itself)
2. A kinematic-tree term (force and motion transmission across edges via incidence matrix $E_m$)
3. A low-rank correction term (long-range coupling between torso and extremities, or global contacts)
The final state transition is computed as $Z_{t+1} = Z_t + \mathcal{A}_{m,t} \bar{B}_t$.

4.5 Paired-Morphology Supervision for Role Separation:
Structural separation alone risks having the network absorb morphology discrepancies inside the basis. To counteract this, pairs of morphology variants are sampled with identical poses and action sequences, and their respective operators are applied to a shared local basis under a paired-morphology loss. This forces the operator pathway to carry dynamics shifts stemming from morphology.

4.6 Reward, Value, and Action Heads:
Task goal embeddings are routed only to reward and value functions, remaining isolated from transition dynamics. Rewards are split into global terms (forward progress, posture maintenance) and local terms (contacts, joint torques). Actions are predicted independently per actuator edge, naturally accommodating varying degrees of freedom.

sections.heading: TD-MPC Planning Operating Directly on Variable-Sized Graphs
sections.summary: TD-MPC-style model predictive control is extended to accommodate graph-structured models. Even when node and actuator counts differ across morphologies, sampling-based action planning runs naturally without fixed-dimension padding.
sections.details:
Latent planning techniques like TD-MPC do not fundamentally require fixed-dimensional latent vectors or fixed action space sizes. At any single decision step, the target robot morphology $m$ is uniquely determined, and its body and actuator counts are known.

In model predictive control (MPC) with GraphOp-WM, action sequences are sampled according to the number of actuators of the current morphology $m$. The current graph state is replicated across the batch dimension, and GraphOp-WM unrolls future trajectory rollouts.

Candidate trajectories are scored by cumulative rewards and terminal values, and an optimal action sequence is obtained via standard sampling-based optimization loops like MPPI (Model Predictive Path Integral) or CEM (Cross-Entropy Method). Without relying on unnatural zero-padding to maximum actuator limits, the framework achieves efficient parallel rollouts while staying faithful to the robot's physical tensor dimensions.

sections.heading: A Systematic Benchmark Sweeping Physical Parameters
sections.summary: Using Hopper, Walker2d, and HalfCheetah, an evaluation environment was constructed by systematically scaling geometry, mass, damping, and gear ratios. Dividing evaluation sets into interpolation, extrapolation, and compositional splits enables rigorous testing of true model generalization.
sections.details:
To validate the generalization ability of the proposed method, a new evaluation benchmark was defined across three representative locomotion environments in the MuJoCo physics engine: Hopper, Walker2d, and HalfCheetah.

In each environment, multiplicative scaling factors were applied to physical parameters of the standard baseline model (MJCF) to generate diverse morphology variants. Specifically manipulated parameters include:
- Link geometry (lengths and radii)
- Link masses and torso mass
- Joint damping coefficients
- Actuator gear ratios
*Note: Rigid body inertia tensors are automatically recalculated from the modified geometry and mass to maintain physical consistency.

Careful attention was paid to parameter splitting. The training set is generated using Latin-hypercube sampling to cover the parameter space uniformly. In contrast, the test set is split into three distinct categories:
1. Interpolation: Parameter values and combinations within the training envelope, but unseen during training.
2. Extrapolation: Parameter values clearly exceeding upper or lower training bounds.
3. Compositional: Held-out combinations where individual parameter ranges were seen during training, but never paired together simultaneously.

Ground friction coefficients, gravitational acceleration, simulation timesteps, termination criteria, and reward formulations are held constant within each family, ensuring that the model's robustness against pure morphological changes is rigorously isolated.

sections.heading: Summary and Outlook: The Promise of Structurally Grounded World Models
sections.summary: GraphOp-WM advances world model generalization across physical parameter shifts. Separating local bases from structured operators provides a powerful inductive bias bridging physics simulators and neural networks.
sections.details:
This paper presented GraphOp-WM, a structured world model designed to achieve morphology-parameter generalization in continuous control. By formulating robots as attributed graphs and factorizing transition dynamics into a morphology-independent local dynamics basis and a static-parameter-conditioned structured operator, it achieves high predictive accuracy and planning performance on unseen physical changes.

Architectural information separation, RMS basis normalization, and contrastive paired-morphology supervision serve as key components to ground this physical division of labor in the learned model.

As the authors highlight, GraphOp-WM does not aim to be a universal controller capable of running arbitrary robot shapes with a single model. Rather, it is designed as a structured inductive bias for compact, high-precision adaptation against hardware variances, wear-and-tear, or component swaps within robot families sharing identical topologies. It marks an important step toward world models that unite physical interpretability with control capabilities.

takeaways: Supplying morphology parameters merely as context vectors is insufficient; structuring them as operators governing motion propagation is key to generalization.

Successfully assigning model roles requires combining architectural information separation—shielding static attributes from dynamic encoders—with paired-morphology supervision sharing identical bases.
Leveraging graph representations aligned with robot topologies allows direct application of MPC (TD-MPC) across variants with differing degrees of freedom and actuator counts without padding.
Evaluating world model generalization demands rigorous benchmark design separating interpolation, extrapolation, and compositional splits, rather than naive random splits.
limitations: Specialized for parameter shifts within the same robot family sharing joint connectivity topology; fundamental structural changes, such as quadruped-to-biped transfer, remain out of scope.
The operator's low-rank correction term approximates ground contacts and long-range couplings, but cannot replicate complex discontinuous contact events with the fidelity of an exact physics solver.
Assumes detailed static parameters (e.g., via CAD or MJCF) are known beforehand, and does not address online parameter identification from interaction when specifications are unknown.
